overallAssessment.verdict: The llyn-peninsula.ts file has a sound thematic structure and captures the peninsula's character (remote, fiercely Welsh-speaking, surf/pilgrimage destination) well in the heroContent. However the content is significantly thinner than comparable region pages: only 4 FAQs (vs 10 for Anglesey), only 2 hiddenGems, only 2 localEatsAndDrinks, and only 5 insiderTips. Key factual claims — the 100-mile coast path, the 70%+ Welsh-first-language figure, the '150 stone huts / 1800 years old' at Tre'r Ceiri, and the AONB designation year — need verification against official sources. All pricing (surfing lessons, Bardsey boat trip, kayaking) is unverified and likely AI-generated. The hero image has no provenance record. There is also an operator discrepancy between llyn-peninsula.ts (which references 'West Coast Surf' in a FAQ) and the surfing combo page (which references 'Hell's Mouth Surf School'). The content/regions/llyn-peninsula.md is a lighter editorial piece but is broadly consistent in tone.
overallAssessment.structuralQuality: MEDIUM — the TS data file covers hero prose, keyFacts, bestFor (10 activities), seasonGuide (4 seasons), 5 insiderTips, 6 topExperiences, 4 FAQs, 2 hiddenGems, 2 localEatsAndDrinks, and SEO meta. These sections are notably thinner than other region pages in the same dataset. FAQs, hiddenGems, and localEatsAndDrinks need expansion before this page can be signed off.

aonbStatus_1956.claim: Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, Designated 1956
aonbStatus_1956.verdict: BROADLY CORRECT — The Llŷn AONB was designated in 1956 under the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act 1949. However, note that AONBs in Wales are in the process of being rebranded as 'Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty' (the branding is retained in Wales, unlike in England where the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 renamed them 'National Landscapes'). The Welsh Government / NRW continues to use AONB designation. Verify current preferred terminology for Wales.
aonbStatus_1956.confidence: HIGH for designation year; MEDIUM for current branding/terminology

coastPath_100miles.verdict: NEEDS_VERIFICATION — '100 miles' is a round figure commonly used in promotional materials, but official Wales Coast Path documentation and NRW materials for the Llŷn Peninsula typically cite approximately 82–84 miles (132–135 km) for the coast path around the peninsula. Some older or broader definitions include sections to Caernarfon that reach closer to 100 miles. The exact figure should be checked against the official Wales Coast Path website before publication.

bardseyIsland_20000saints.claim: Island of 20,000 Saints, Medieval pilgrimage destination, boat trips
bardseyIsland_20000saints.verdict: VERIFIED (name and heritage status) — Bardsey Island (Ynys Enlli) is traditionally known as the 'Isle of 20,000 Saints' (Ynys y 20,000 o Saint), referencing medieval pilgrims and monks buried there. Three pilgrimages to Bardsey was traditionally said to equal one pilgrimage to Rome. The island is managed by the Bardsey Island Trust (Ymddiriedolaeth Ynys Enlli). Day trips (weather permitting) run from Porth Meudwy, near Aberdaron. Overnight stays available in the island farmhouse.
bardseyIsland_20000saints.note: The boat crossing from Porth Meudwy to Bardsey is approximately 2 miles but is weather-dependent. The Bardsey Bird and Field Observatory (BBFO) adds to the island's wildlife appeal.

hellsMouth_4miles.claim: Porth Neigwl (Hell's Mouth), 4 miles of sand, consistent Atlantic swell
hellsMouth_4miles.verdict: APPROXIMATELY CORRECT — Porth Neigwl is widely described as 4 miles (6.4 km) in length and faces south-southwest, making it one of the most reliable swell-catching beaches in North Wales. It is exposed to Atlantic swells from the southwest. The '4 miles' figure appears in NRW, Visit Wales, and multiple surf media sources.

welshLanguage_70percent.claim: 70%+ first language, One of the most Welsh-speaking areas
welshLanguage_70percent.verdict: NEEDS_VERIFICATION — The Llŷn Peninsula (Pen Llŷn) is one of Wales's most Welsh-speaking areas. The 2021 Census for Gwynedd as a whole recorded 65.1% able to speak Welsh. Specific Llŷn communities (e.g. Aberdaron, Tudweiliog, Llanbedrog) may individually exceed 70%, but the peninsula-wide '70%+ first language' claim needs verification against 2021 Census ward-level data. The 2011 Census did show several Llŷn wards at 72–80% Welsh-speaking.

welshLanguage_70percent.confidence: MEDIUM — directionally correct; specific claim needs 2021 ward-level data

trerCeiri_hillfort.claim: Iron Age hillfort, 150 stone huts, 1800 years old
trerCeiri_hillfort.verdict: PARTIALLY CORRECT — Tre'r Ceiri (Town of Giants) is one of the best-preserved Iron Age hillforts in Britain, situated on the Yr Eifl (The Rivals) ridge. The '150 stone huts' figure is commonly cited in Welsh heritage sources and is plausible, though RCAHMW (Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales) records over 150 stone house platforms. The '1800 years old' claim is misleading: the site was first occupied c. 200 BC and continued into the Romano-British period to c. 400 AD. From 2026, 1800 years points to approximately 226 AD — the later Romano-British phase. The original hillfort construction is over 2000 years old. '1800 years old' undersells the site's antiquity.
trerCeiri_hillfort.action: Update llyn-peninsula.ts to: 'over 150 stone house platforms, occupied from approximately 200 BC to 400 AD' — this is both more accurate and more impressive than '1800 years old'.
trerCeiri_hillfort.confidence: MEDIUM — '150 huts' directionally correct; '1800 years old' misleading

distanceFromSnowdonia_30to45min.verdict: APPROXIMATELY CORRECT — Driving from the Snowdonia boundary (e.g. Caernarfon or Porthmadog) to Abersoch or Aberdaron takes 40–55 minutes on narrow A/B roads. '30-45 minutes' is slightly optimistic for driving to the western tip but reasonable for the eastern entry point near Pwllheli.

population_20000.verdict: PLAUSIBLE — The Llŷn Peninsula does not correspond to a single administrative unit, making precise population verification difficult. The sub-area of Pen Llŷn in Gwynedd County Council is a broadly agricultural peninsula. Gwynedd's total population is approximately 125,000 (2021 Census). A rough estimate of ~20,000 for the peninsula is consistent with the character described and the known settlement pattern. Precise verification would require ward-level data aggregation.
population_20000.confidence: MEDIUM — plausible figure; exact number requires ward-level aggregation

whistlingSands_quartz.claim: Porth Oer's sand squeaks when dry—the quartz grains rub together
whistlingSands_quartz.verdict: VERIFIED — Porth Oer (Whistling Sands) is a National Trust-managed beach known for this acoustic property. The sand is composed predominantly of quartz grains of remarkably uniform size and spherical shape. The sound is a squeak or whistle produced by dry sand friction, not a true whistle. This is described by the National Trust and in multiple geological sources.

verifiedGems.name: Porth Ysgo
verifiedGems.verdict: VERIFIED — Porth Ysgo is a small, secluded cove near Aberdaron on the south coast of Llŷn. Accessed via steep steps down through a valley owned by the National Trust. Excellent wild swimming. Correctly described.

verifiedGems.name: St Beuno's Church, Clynnog Fawr
verifiedGems.verdict: BROADLY CORRECT — St Beuno's is a 16th-century collegiate church at Clynnog Fawr on the north side of the Llŷn Peninsula. It was an important stopping point on the Pilgrim's Way to Bardsey Island. The '16th-century' attribution refers to the current church building; a religious site has existed here since the 6th century when St Beuno established his community. The church contains a holy well (Ffynnon Beuno) separate from the church building.

additionalHiddenGemCandidates.description: National Trust-owned fishing village and beach on the north coast, accessible only on foot (1-mile walk from Morfa Nefyn). Home to the Ty Coch Inn. Stunning bay. Frequently cited as one of Wales's most beautiful spots.

additionalHiddenGemCandidates.name: Mynydd Mawr (Braich y Pwll)
additionalHiddenGemCandidates.description: The headland at the very tip of the Llŷn Peninsula, south of Aberdaron. Views to Bardsey Island, dramatic cliffs, and the crossing where pilgrims traditionally departed. Wild and largely unvisited.

additionalHiddenGemCandidates.name: Porth Iago
additionalHiddenGemCandidates.description: Secluded NT-owned cove on the north coast with turquoise water. Privately accessible via a farm track. One of the Llŷn's best-kept secrets.

additionalHiddenGemCandidates.name: Nant Gwrtheyrn (Welsh Language Centre)
additionalHiddenGemCandidates.description: Former granite quarrying village in a dramatic valley on Yr Eifl, now a Welsh language and heritage centre. The village itself is remarkable: accessible via a steep single-track road into the valley.

markdownVsTsAudit.verdict: The two files are broadly consistent in character and key assets named. No direct factual conflicts identified. The markdown (content/regions/llyn-peninsula.md) is a lighter editorial piece (~500 words) in a conversational tone. Key differences:
observations: The markdown's 'What It's NOT Good For' section explicitly says 'If you're after adrenaline-pumping activities like mountain biking or hardcore climbing... head to Snowdonia.' The TS data file does not make this contrast, and the bestFor list is broader (includes heritage, wild swimming, stargazing). The markdown underplays the adventure dimension relative to the TS data file.

The markdown's 'Smart Play' section recommends basing in or around Aberdaron and lists Whistling Sands, Porth Oer (same beach, correctly cross-referenced), and a Bardsey boat trip. This matches the TS data file recommendations.

The markdown does not mention Tre'r Ceiri, Hell's Mouth surfing (beyond a brief watersports mention), or the Llŷn Coastal Path. These are material omissions in the shorter editorial piece — the markdown should be supplemented if it is the primary editorial content.
The markdown spells the beach as 'Porth Oer' rather than 'Porth Oer (Whistling Sands)' — minor but the Whistling Sands name is the more commonly searched term and should appear.
markdownVsTsAudit.recommendation: The llyn-peninsula.ts data is the canonical source for structured content. The markdown is a thin editorial introduction. No conflicts requiring resolution were identified, but the markdown should be updated to better reflect the adventure dimension before sign-off.
